title: Edge cases and testing
summary: Hunt for the inputs that break code, and check your work with examples you choose on purpose.

steps.title: Where bugs hide
body: Code usually works for the "normal" input you had in mind. Bugs hide at the **edges**. Ask of every function:
- **Empty**: an empty list, an empty string, zero.
- **Boundaries**: the exact value where a rule changes (`age == 18`, the last index).
- **Duplicates and ties**: two equal largest values.
- **Bad input**: `null`, text where a number was expected.
These categories are the same whatever language you write in.

steps.prompt: For `int Average(int[] nums)`, is each test input a **normal** case or an **edge** case?
steps.explain: The empty list divides by zero, the huge values overflow the sum, `[-3, 3]` averages to zero, and one item tests the smallest real input.

steps.prompt: This average looks fine. Run it on an edge case: what is printed?
code: foreach (int n in nums) sum += n;
steps.explain: The sum overflows to -2, and -2 / 2 is -1. A `long` sum fixes it. This is why you test the extremes.

steps.title: Test with examples you chose
body: A **test** is a call with a known right answer: *given this input, I expect this output*. Write them **before or while** you code, choosing examples from each edge category.
A good set of tests is small but **varied**: each test should be able to catch a mistake the others would miss. Ten tests that are all "normal" catch less than three well-chosen ones.

steps.prompt: This `IsSorted` has a bug. Which test would catch it?
steps.explain: The `else return true` stops after checking only the first pair. You need a test where the first pair is fine and a *later* pair is not.

steps.prompt: For a function `Grade(int score)` where 50 and above passes, match each edge category to the test input that covers it.
steps.explain: Testing 49 and 50 together pins down whether the code used `>` or `>=`, the most common boundary bug.

steps.title: Fix it with the tests
prompt: Fix `IsSorted` so it checks **every** neighbouring pair. Arrays with zero or one item count as sorted. Equal neighbours are fine (`[1, 1, 2]` is sorted).
template: Dojo.Eq("[1, 2, 0] is not sorted", false, IsSorted(new[] { 1, 2, 0 }));
Dojo.Eq("[] is sorted", true, IsSorted(new int[0]));
hints: You can only say "sorted" after you have looked at **every** pair.
Delete the `else` branch so the loop keeps going.

steps.title: Delve's own tests
prompt: A game you keep changing needs tests, so that a change in March does not quietly break a fight you wrote in January. Write Delve's checks for three of your pieces. In the real game, **`dotnet run -- check`** runs them against your own code.
- **`static void Expect(List<string> failures, string name, bool ok)`** adds `name` to `failures` when `ok` is false.
- **`static List<string> DelveChecks()`** makes an empty list, calls `Expect` once per check, and returns the list (empty means everything passed).
Write **at least 8 checks** covering the normal cases **and the edges** of:
- `Heal(hp, amount, maxHp)`: healing below the max, at the max, and a potion of `int.MaxValue`.
- `Damage(attack, armour)`: armour that blocks fully, armour that runs out, a hit too weak to be blocked.
- `MoveOutcome(map, x, y, stairsOpen)`: a wall, a floor tile, and points **off the map on every side** (a crash is a failed check too).

How you are graded: the checks run your tests against the correct pieces (they must all pass) and against **seven broken versions** that each hide a different bug. Your tests must catch every one. Think like the bug: what would a careless version of each function get wrong?
starter: static void Expect(List<string> failures, string name, bool ok)
solution: static void Expect(List<string> failures, string name, bool ok)
Expect(failures, "heal survives a huge potion", Heal(5, int.MaxValue, 20) == 20);
Expect(failures, "armour blocks every third point", Damage(9, 5) == 6);
Expect(failures, "armour blocks no more than it has", Damage(9, 1) == 8);
Expect(failures, "a weak hit still lands", Damage(2, 4) == 2);
Expect(failures, "the floor is walkable", MoveOutcome(room, 1, 1, false) == "move");
Expect(failures, "off the map is blocked, not a crash", MoveOutcome(room, -1, 1, false) == "blocked");
Expect(failures, "far off the map too", MoveOutcome(room, 1, 3, false) == "blocked");
template: catch (Exception e) { return new List<string> { "crashed: " + e.GetType().Name }; }
Dojo.Check("all your checks pass on the correct pieces", dojoGood.Count == 0, "these failed on correct code: " + string.Join(", ", dojoGood));
"Heal adds in an int and overflows",
"Damage blocks every third point without the armour limit",
"MoveOutcome reads the tile before checking the edges",
"MoveOutcome forgets the bottom and right edges",
Dojo.Check("catches: " + dojoBugs[dojoMode], DojoRun(dojoMode).Count > 0, "every check passed on this broken version");
static int Heal(int hp, int amount, int maxHp)
static int Damage(int attack, int armour)
static string MoveOutcome(string[] map, int x, int y, bool stairsOpen)
bool outside = DojoBug.Mode == 6 ? x < 0 || y < 0 : x < 0 || y < 0 || x >= map[0].Length || y >= map.Length;
static class DojoBug { public static int Mode; }

forbid.message: Every function starts with `static` (Delve keeps its pieces in one static class)
Tests the game's pieces, does not write new ones

steps.explain: Run `dotnet run -- check` in your Delve space: the same checks now guard your own pieces every time you change them.
